feed_card.headline: Bacteria were said to outnumber your cells 10 to 1. Counted properly, it is about 1.3 to 1.
teasers: A textbook number that was never counted
Most of your cells carry no DNA
Why the microbiome craze leaned on it

sections.content: Bacteria were said to outnumber your cells 10 to 1. Counted properly, it is about 1.3 to 1.

sections.content: The figure sounds like it came from a microscope. It came from arithmetic. In 1972 a researcher multiplied a rough count of bacteria per gram by a rough gut volume, reached about a hundred trillion microbes, set that beside the standard guess of ten trillion body cells, and wrote 10 to 1. Nobody had counted either number. The line spread from that single paper into reviews, textbooks, and popular science, picking up authority it was never given. A team finally tallied both totals in 2016, and the chasm closed: roughly 38 trillion bacteria against 30 trillion human cells, about 1.3 to 1.

items: About 84% of your 30 trillion human cells are red blood cells: tiny, disc-shaped, and carrying no nucleus and no DNA.
Count only the cells that keep a nucleus, roughly a tenth of the total, and bacteria run well ahead of them again.

sections.content: The 2016 recount worked tissue by tissue. For the human side, Ron Milo's group at the Weizmann Institute added up the body's cell types from anatomical data. One type swamped the rest. Red blood cells, counted from total blood volume, make up the large majority of you by cell number. For the bacteria, the team went to the colon, where nearly all of them live, and multiplied a measured density of microbes per gram of contents by the measured volume of the gut. It is the same move made in 1972, now with real numbers instead of round ones, and the two totals came out within about 30% of each other.

content.body: In 1972 Thomas Luckey, a nutritionist who had spent years raising germ-free animals, needed a number for how many microbes live in a human gut. He took a plausible figure for bacteria per gram and multiplied it by the gut's rough capacity, landing on about a hundred trillion. It was a back-of-an-envelope guess, and he offered it as one. Five years later a widely cited review by Dwayne Savage repeated the figure, and from there it set. Each paper leaned on the one before, the hedges fell away, and a rough estimate turned into common knowledge. Not until 2016 did Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs, and Ron Milo add both sides up carefully, and when they did, the ratio came out near one to one.

key_figures.name: Ron Milo
key_figures.one_line: His group at the Weizmann Institute counted both cell populations and put the ratio at about 1.3 to 1.

content.title: The count is a flow, not a fixed number
content.body: Nearly all of those bacteria sit in the colon, and the colon empties. The 2016 paper notes that each bowel movement clears out a quarter to a third of its contents, so the bacterial total swings by trillions across a single day. The number is a moving average of a population that is constantly being flushed and regrown. Treating it as a fixed constant was part of what made the old ratio feel more solid than it was.

content.title: The old number survived because nobody reran it
content.body: A rough estimate is not a mistake; offering one is normal science. The failure came after. For four decades the figure was passed from paper to paper by citation, not by measurement, and each pass stripped away the hedges the original carried. By the time it reached the general public it had the ring of a settled fact, and settled facts do not get rechecked. The recount was overdue by the day it was published.

sections.content: The microbiome still matters. Those bacteria train the immune system, digest what we cannot, and help build the gut lining, and none of that depends on the exact ratio. The recount did not shrink any of it. What it corrected was a slogan: the claim that we are more microbe than human, only 10% ourselves, built on a figure nobody had measured. The bacteria are still there in their tens of trillions, doing that work. They just about match your own cells while they do it.

content.question: Why is the old 10-to-1 claim now considered unreliable?
options: It rested on a single rough calculation, with neither cell population counted
The study behind it was later retracted for fraud
It measured bacteria in the mouth rather than the gut
It accidentally counted viruses as bacteria
content.explanation: The figure came from a 1972 back-of-the-envelope estimate that multiplied a rough bacterial density by a rough gut volume. No one had tallied the human cells or the bacteria.

content.question: The careful 2016 recount put the bacteria-to-human ratio at roughly...
options: 10 to 1
1 to 10
content.explanation: About 38 trillion bacteria against 30 trillion human cells lands near 1.3 to 1, close enough to call it roughly even rather than a tenfold gap.

content.question: Most of your 30 trillion human cells are which type?
options: Neurons
Skin cells
Muscle cells
Red blood cells, which carry no nucleus
content.explanation: Red blood cells make up about 84% of the human cell count. They are among the smallest cells in the body and carry no nucleus and no DNA.

content.question: Why does counting only nucleated human cells change the comparison so much?
options: Nucleated cells are heavier, so they dominate by mass
Red blood cells are the vast majority, so removing them leaves far fewer human cells to compare
Bacteria also lack nuclei, so the two cancel out
Nucleated cells divide faster and keep multiplying
content.explanation: Around 90% of human cells are red blood cells and platelets with no nucleus. Count only the remaining tenth and the human total collapses, leaving bacteria well ahead.

content.question: How did a rough guess survive as fact for decades?
options: Repeated experiments kept confirming it
No instrument could check it until 2016
Each paper cited the previous one until the estimate read as established
A scientific body formally ratified the number
content.explanation: The figure spread by citation rather than measurement. With every pass the original hedges dropped away, and a hedged estimate hardened into common knowledge.

content.question: Does the corrected ratio mean the microbiome is unimportant?
options: Yes, the bacteria turned out to be negligible
Yes, human cells do all the real work
No, because bacteria still outnumber us 10 to 1
No, the bacteria still shape immunity and digestion; only the outnumbering slogan was wrong
content.explanation: The importance of gut bacteria never hinged on the ratio. The recount corrected a talking point, not the biology of what the microbiome does.

content.myth: If the ratio is not 10 to 1, the whole microbiome idea was hype.
content.reality: The bacteria still number in the tens of trillions and do real work. The recount changed the comparison, not the biology.

content.myth: The true ratio is exactly one to one.
content.reality: The best figure is about 1.3 to 1 for a standard adult, and it runs higher in a small child. Roughly even is the honest claim; a clean 1 to 1 is not.

content.myth: A better count later could push it back toward 10 to 1.
content.reality: It will not budge that far. The 2016 figure rests on measured densities and volumes with an uncertainty around 25%, nowhere near the order of magnitude the old number was off by.
